title: Example
body_md:
Consider a counting query $f$, namely a function that, applied to a dataset $x$, returns the number of individuals in $x$ that satisfy a given property. A way to implement differential privacy \cite{Dwork:06:TCC} is to add geometrical noise to the result of $f$, so to obtain a probability distribution $P$ on integers of the form $P(z) = c \, e^{|z-f(x)|}$, where $c$ is a normalization factor. The resulting mechanism can  be interpreted as a probabilistic choice on protocols of the form $f(x), f(x) + 1, f(x) + 2, \ldots , f(x) - 1, f(x)-2, \ldots$, where the probability assigned to 
 $f(x) + n$ and to $f(x)-n$ decreases exponentially with $n$.
head: environment
name: Differential privacy

title: Example
body_md:
Consider two agents running the dining cryptographers protocol \cite{Chaum:88:JC}, which consists in tossing a fair binary coin and then declaring 
the exclusive or $\oplus$ of their secret value $x$ and the result of the coin.  The protocol can be thought as the fair probabilistic choice  of two protocols, one consisting simply of declaring $x$, and the other declaring $x\oplus 1$.
head: environment
name: Dining cryptographers

label: exe:Crime
title: Example
body_md:
\label{exe:Crime}
Compression Ratio Info-leak Made Easy (CRIME) \cite{Rizzo:12:Ekoparty} is a
security exploit against secret web cookies over connections using the HTTPS and SPDY protocols and  data compression. 
The idea is that the attacker can inject some content $a$ in the communication of the secret $x$ from the target site to the server. The server then compresses and  encrypts the data, including both $a$ and $x$, and sends back the result. By observing the length of the result, the attacker can then infer information about $x$. 
To mitigate the leakage, one possible defense would consist in transmitting, along with $x$, also an encryption method $f$ selected randomly from a set $F$. Again, the resulting protocol can be seen as a composition, using probabilistic choice, of the protocols in the set $F$.
head: environment
name: CRIME attack

label: ex:Timing
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:Timing}
Consider a password-checker, or any similar system in which the user authenticates himself
by entering a secret that is checked by the system. An adversary does not know the real secret,
of course, but a timing side-channel could reveal the \emph{part} (eg. which bit) of the secret in which the adversary's
input fails. By repeating the process with different inputs, the adversary might be able to
fully retrieve the secret. A possible counter measure is to make the side channel noisy,
by randomizing the order in which the secret's bit are checked against the user input.
This example is studied in detaul in Section~\ref{sec:password-example}.
head: environment
name: Timing side-channels

label: theo:vonneumann
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theo:vonneumann}
Let $\mathcal{X} \subset \mathbb{R}^m$ and $\mathcal{Y} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be compact convex sets,
and $\textit{U}: \mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be a continuous function such that
$\textit{U}(x, y)$ is a convex function in $x\in\mathcal{X}$ and a concave function in $y\in\mathcal{Y}$.
Then
\[
\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}} \max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}} \textit{U}(x, y) = \max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}} \min_{x\in\mathcal{X}} \textit{U}(x, y)
.
\]
head: environment
name: von Neumann's minimax theorem

label: prop:type-hidden-choice
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:type-hidden-choice}
Given a family $\{C_{i}\}_{i \in \mathcal{I}}$ of 
channels of  type $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, 
and a distribution $\mu$ on $\mathcal{I}$, 
the hidden choice 
${\osum_{i \leftarrow \mu}} C_{i}$ is 
a channel of type
$\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$.
head: environment
name: Type of hidden choice

label: prop:type-visible-choice
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:type-visible-choice}
Given a family $\{C_{i}\}_{i \in \mathcal{I}}$ of 
compatible channels s.t. each $C_{i}$ has type 
$\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}_{i} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$,
and a distribution $\mu$ on $\mathcal{I}$, 
the result of the visible choice 
${\bigsqcupdot_{i \leftarrow \mu}} C_{i}$ is a channel
of type 
$\mathcal{X} \times \left( \bigsqcup_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \mathcal{Y}_{i} \right) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$.
head: environment
name: Type of visible choice

label: def:equivalence-channels
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:equivalence-channels}
Two compatible channels $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$
with domain $\mathcal{X}$
are \emph{equivalent}, denoted by $C_{1} \approx C_{2}$,
if for every prior $\pi \in \mathbb{D}{\mathcal{X}}$ and every 
posterior vulnerability $\mathbb{V}$ we have
               
$
\mathbb{V}\left[\pi,C_{1}\right] = \mathbb{V}\left[\pi,C_{2}\right]
$.
head: environment
name: Equivalence of channels

label: prop:idempotency
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:idempotency}
Given a family $\{C_{i}\}_{i \in \mathcal{I}}$ of 
channels s.t. $C_{i} = C$ for all $i \in \mathcal{I}$,
and a distribution $\mu$ on $\mathcal{I}$, then:
                     
                      
      
(a) ${{\osum_{i \leftarrow \mu}}C_{i} = C}$; and
       
(b) ${{\bigsqcupdot_{i \leftarrow \mu}}C_{i} \approx C}$.

label: theo:convex-V-q
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theo:convex-V-q}
Let $\{C_{i}\}_{i \in \mathcal{I}}$ be a family of channels,
and $\mu$ be a distribution on $\mathcal{I}$.
Then, for every distribution $\pi$ on $\mathcal{X}$, and every
vulnerability $\mathbb{V}$:
\begin{enumerate}
\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item \label{enumerate:vg:h:convex}
posterior vulnerability is convex w.r.t. to hidden choice:
               
$
\mathbb{V}\left[\pi,{\osum_{i \leftarrow \mu}} C_{i}\right] \leq \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \mu(i) \,\mathbb{V}\left[\pi,C_{i}\right]
$
             
if all $C_{i}$'s have the same type.

\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item \label{enumerate:vg:v:linear}
posterior vulnerability is linear w.r.t. to visible choice:
               
$
\mathbb{V}\left[\pi,{\bigsqcupdot_{i \leftarrow \mu}} C_{i}\right] = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \mu(i) \,\mathbb{V}\left[\pi,C_{i}\right]
$
             
if all $C_{i}$'s are compatible.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Convexity/linearity of posterior vulnerability w.r.t. choices

label: cor:concave-convex-V
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:concave-convex-V}
Let $\{C_{i j}\}_{i \in \mathcal{I}, j \in \mathcal{J}}$ be a family of channels,
all with domain $\mathcal{X}$ and with the same type, and let $\pi\in \mathbb{D}\mathcal{X}$, and $\mathbb{V}$ be any vulnerability. 
Define
$\textit{U}: \mathbb{D}\mathcal{I}\times\mathbb{D}\mathcal{J}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ as follows:
               
$
\textit{U}(\mu, \eta) \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}} \mathbb{V}\left[\pi,{\osum_{i \leftarrow \mu}} \; {\bigsqcupdot_{j \leftarrow \eta}} \; C_{i j}\right]
$.
             
Then $\textit{U}$ is convex on $\mu$ and linear on $\eta$.
head: environment
name: Convex-linear payoff function

label: theo:deterministic-strategies-II
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theo:deterministic-strategies-II}
Consider a defender-first sequential game with visible choice, and attacker's strategies of type 
$\mathbb{D}(\mathcal{D}\,{\rightarrow}\,\mathcal{A})$. Let $d^*\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}} \operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_d \max_a \textit{u}(d,a)$ and let $\textit{s}_{\sf a}^*:\mathcal{D}\,{\rightarrow}\,\mathcal{A}$ be defined as $\textit{s}_{\sf a}^*(d)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}}  \operatornamewithlimits{argmax}_{a} \textit{u}(d,a)$
(if there is more than one  $a$ that maximizes $\textit{u}(d,a)$, we select one of them arbitrarily). 
Then   
for every $\delta\in\mathbb{D}\mathcal{D}$ and ${\sigma_{\sf a}}\in\mathbb{D}(\mathcal{D}\,{\rightarrow}\,\mathcal{A})$ we have
$
\textit{U}(d^*,{\sigma_{\sf a}})\leq \textit{u}(d^*,\textit{s}_{\sf a}^*(d^*))\leq \textit{U}(\delta,\textit{s}_{\sf a}^*)
$.
head: environment
name: Pure-strategy Nash equilibrium in Game II -  strategies of type $\distr(\calda)$

title: Example
body_md:
Consider  the example of Section~\ref{sec:running-example} in the setting of Game II, with uniform prior.
If the defender chooses $0$ then the attacker chooses $1$. 
If the defender chooses $1$ then the attacker chooses $0$.
In both cases, the payoff is $1$. The game has therefore two solutions, $(\delta^*_1,\alpha^*_1)$ and $(\delta^*_2,\alpha^*_2)$, 
with $\delta^*_1(0)=1$, $\alpha^*_1(0)=0$ and $\delta^*_2(0)=0$, $\alpha^*_2(1)=1$.
head: environment

label: theo:deterministic-strategies-II-2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theo:deterministic-strategies-II-2}
Consider a defender-first sequential game with visible choice, and attacker's strategies of type 
$\mathcal{D} \rightarrow \mathbb{D}(\mathcal{A})$.
Let $d^*\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}} \operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_d \max_a \textit{u}(d,a)$ and let $\phi^*_{\sf a}:\mathcal{D} \rightarrow \mathbb{D}(\mathcal{A})$ be defined as $\phi^*_{\sf a}(d)(a)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}} 1$ if $a= \operatornamewithlimits{argmax}_{a'} \textit{u}(d,a')$ (if there is more than one such $a$, we select one of them arbitrarily), and $\phi^*_{\sf a}(d)(a)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}} 0$ otherwise. 
Then   
for every $\delta\in\mathbb{D}\mathcal{D}$ and ${\phi_{\sf a}}: \mathcal{D} \rightarrow \mathbb{D}(\mathcal{A})$ we have:
$
\textit{U}(d^*,{\phi_{\sf a}}(d^*))\leq \textit{U}(d^*,\phi^*_{\sf a}(d^*))\leq \textit{U}(\delta,\phi^*_{\sf a})
$.
head: environment
name: Pure-strategy Nash equilibrium in Game II - strategies of type $\cald \rightarrow \distr(\cala)$

label: coro:equivalence-II
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{coro:equivalence-II}
Consider a defender-first sequential game with visible choice, and let $d^*$, $\textit{s}_{\sf a}^*$ and $\phi^*_{\sf a}$ be defined as in Theorems~\ref{theo:deterministic-strategies-II} and \ref{theo:deterministic-strategies-II-2} respectively. 
Then   
$
\textit{u}(d^*,\textit{s}_{\sf a}^*(d^*))= \textit{U}(d^*,\phi^*_{\sf a}(d^*)).
$
head: environment
name: Equivalence of optimal strategies of types $\distr(\calda)$ and $\cald \rightarrow \distr(\cala)$ in Game II

label: theo:deterministic-strategies-III
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theo:deterministic-strategies-III}
Consider a defender-first sequential game with visible choice. 
Let $a^*\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}} \operatornamewithlimits{argmax}_a \min_d \textit{u}(d,a)$. Let $\textit{s}_{\sf d}^*:\mathcal{A}\,{\rightarrow}\,\mathcal{D}$ be defined as $\textit{s}_{\sf d}^*(a)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}}  \operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{d} \textit{u}(d,a)$, and 
let $\phi^*_{\sf d}:\mathcal{A} \rightarrow \mathbb{D}(\mathcal{D})$ be defined as $\phi^*_{\sf d}(a)(d)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}} 1$ if $d= \operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{d'} \textit{u}(d',a)$. 
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item For every $\alpha\in\mathbb{D}\mathcal{A}$ and ${\sigma_{\sf d}}\in\mathbb{D}(\mathcal{A}\,{\rightarrow}\,\mathcal{D})$ we have
$
\textit{U}(\textit{s}_{\sf d}^*,\alpha)\leq \textit{u}(\textit{s}_{\sf d}^*(a^*),a^*)\leq \textit{U}({\sigma_{\sf d}},a^*)
$.\\[-1ex]
\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item For every $\alpha\in\mathbb{D}\mathcal{A}$ and ${\phi_{\sf d}}: \mathcal{A} \rightarrow \mathbb{D}(\mathcal{D})$ we have:
$
\textit{U}(\phi^*_{\sf d},\alpha)\leq \textit{U}(\phi^*_{\sf d}(a^*),a^*)\leq \textit{U}({\phi_{\sf d}}(a^*),a^*)
$.\\[-1ex]
\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item $\textit{u}(\textit{s}_{\sf d}^*(a^*),a^*)= \textit{U}(\phi^*_{\sf d}(a^*),a^*)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Pure-strategy Nash equilibria in Game  III and equivalence of $ \distr(\calad)$ and  $(\cala\rightarrow \distr(\cald))$

title: Example
body_md:
Consider now the example of Section~\ref{sec:running-example} in the setting of Game III, with uniform prior.
If the attacker chooses $0$ then the defender chooses $0$ and the payoff is $\nicefrac{1}{2}$.  
If the attacker chooses $1$ then the defender  chooses $1$ and the payoff is $\nicefrac{2}{3}$.
The latter case is more convenient for the attacker, hence the solution of the game is the strategy profile $(\delta^*,\alpha^*)$ 
with $\delta^*(0)=0$, $\alpha^*(0)=0$.
head: environment

label: exa:exempio
title: Example
body_md:
\label{exa:exempio}
Consider now the example of Section~\ref{sec:running-example} in the setting of Game IV.
For $\delta\in\mathbb{D}\mathcal{D}$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb{D}\mathcal{A}$, let $p=\delta(0)$ and $q=\alpha(0)$. 
The system can be represented by the channel 
$(C_{00}\;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{10})\;{{}_{q}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\sqcupdot}}}}\;(C_{01}\;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{11})$
represented below.
\begin{align*}
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
C_{00}  \;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{10}& y=0 & y=1 \\ \hline
x=0    & p & \overline{p} \\
x=1    & 1 & 0 \\ \hline
\end{array}
\quad
\;{{}_{q}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\sqcupdot}}}}\;
\quad
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
C_{01}\;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{11}& y=0 & y=1 \\ \hline
x=0    & \nicefrac{1}{3}+ \nicefrac{2}{3}\;p &   \nicefrac{2}{3}- \nicefrac{2}{3}\;p \\
x=1    & \nicefrac{2}{3}- \nicefrac{2}{3}\;p  & \nicefrac{1}{3}+ \nicefrac{2}{3}\,p \\ \hline
\end{array}
\end{align*}
\noindent For uniform $\pi$, we have
$\mathbb{V}\left[\pi, C_{00} \;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{10}\right]{=}1-\nicefrac{1}{2}\,p$, 
while
$\mathbb{V}\left[\pi, C_{10}  \;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{11}\right]$ is equal to
$
\nicefrac{2}{3}- \nicefrac{2}{3}\,p$ if $p\leq \nicefrac{1}{4}$,
and equal to 
$\nicefrac{1}{3}+ \nicefrac{2}{3}\,p$ 
if $p> \nicefrac{1}{4}$.
          
Hence the payoff, expressed in terms of $p$ and $q$, is
$\textit{U}(p,q) = q(1-\nicefrac{1}{2}\,p) + \overline{q} (\nicefrac{2}{3} - \nicefrac{2}{3}\,p)$
if $p\leq \nicefrac{1}{4}$, and 
$\textit{U}(p,q) = q(1-\nicefrac{1}{2}\,p) + \overline{q} (\nicefrac{1}{3} + \nicefrac{2}{3}\,p)$ 
if $p> \nicefrac{1}{4}$.
The Nash equilibrium can be computed by imposing that the partial derivatives of 
$\textit{U}(p,q)$ with respect to $p$ and $q$ are both $0$, which means that we are in a  saddle point.  
We have:
\[
\renewcommand{1}{1.7}
\frac{\partial \textit{U}(p,q)}{\partial q}=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
		\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{6}\,p&, \text{ if } p\leq\frac{1}{4}\\
		\frac{2}{3}-\frac{7}{6}\,p&, \text{ if } p>\frac{1}{4}\\
		\end{array}
		\right.
\qquad
\frac{\partial \textit{U}(p,q)}{\partial p}=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
		-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{6}\,q&, \text{ if } p\leq\frac{1}{4}\\
		\frac{2}{3}-\frac{7}{6}\,q&, \text{ if }  p>\frac{1}{4}\\
		\end{array}
		\right.		
\renewcommand{1}{1}
\]		
We can see that the equations $\nicefrac{\partial \textit{U}(p,q)}{\partial q}=0$ and $\nicefrac{\partial \textit{U}(p,q)}{\partial p}=0$ do not have solutions in $[0,1]$ for $p\leq \nicefrac{1}{4}$, 
while for $p> \nicefrac{1}{4}$ they have solution $p^*=q^*=\nicefrac{4}{7}$.
The pair $(p^*, q^*)$ thus constitutes the Nash equilibrium, and the corresponding payoff is $\textit{U}(p^*,q^*) = \nicefrac{5}{7}$.
head: environment

label: Theo:deterministic solution Game VI
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Theo:deterministic solution Game VI}
Consider an attacker-first sequential game with hidden choice.
\begin{description}
\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item[1. Mixed strategies -- type $\mathbb{D}(\mathcal{A}\,{\rightarrow}\,\mathcal{D})$.] Let  
$a^*\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}} \operatornamewithlimits{argmax}_a\min_{{\sigma_{\sf d}}}\mathbb{V}\left[\pi,{{\osum_{\textit{s}_{\sf d} \leftarrow {\sigma_{\sf d}}}}} {C_{\textit{s}_{\sf d}(a) a}}\right]$, and let 
$\sigma^*_{\sf d}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}}  \operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{{\sigma_{\sf d}}} \lambda a. \mathbb{V}\left[\pi,{{\osum_{\textit{s}_{\sf d} \leftarrow {\sigma_{\sf d}}}}} {C_{\textit{s}_{\sf d}(a) a}}\right]$.
Then, for every $\alpha\in\mathbb{D}\mathcal{A}$ and ${\sigma_{\sf d}}\in\mathbb{D}(\mathcal{A}\,{\rightarrow}\,\mathcal{D})$ we have
\[
\textit{U}(\sigma^*_{\sf d},\alpha)\leq \textit{U}(\sigma^*_{\sf d},a^*)\leq \textit{U}({\sigma_{\sf d}},a^*)
\]
\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item[2. Behavioral strategies -- type $\mathcal{A}\rightarrow \mathbb{D}(\mathcal{D})$.] Let  
$a^*\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}} \operatornamewithlimits{argmax}_a\min_{\delta}\mathbb{V}\left[\pi,{{\osum_{d \leftarrow \delta}}} {C_{d a}}\right]$, and let
$\phi^*_{\sf d}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}}  \operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{{\phi_{\sf d}}} \lambda a. \mathbb{V}\left[\pi,{{\osum_{d \leftarrow {\phi_{\sf d}}(a)}}} {C_{d a}}\right]$. (The minimization is with respect to the point-wise ordering.) 
Then, for every $\alpha\in\mathbb{D}\mathcal{A}$ and ${\phi_{\sf d}}:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow \mathbb{D}(\mathcal{D})$ we have
\[
\textit{U}(\phi^*_{\sf d},\alpha)\leq \textit{U}(\phi^*_{\sf d},a^*)\leq \textit{U}({\phi_{\sf d}},a^*)
\]
\end{description}
head: environment
name: Attacker's pure-strategy Nash equilibrium in Game VI

title: Example
body_md:
Consider the channel matrices $C_{ij}$ defined in Section~\ref{sec:running-example},  and define the 
following new channels: $C'_{00} = C'_{11} = C_{01}$ and  $C'_{10} = C'_{01}= C_{10}$. 
Define $D_p$ as the result of the hidden choice, with probability $p$,  between $C'_{00}$ and  $C'_{10}$, i.e., $D_p \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}} C'_{00}\;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\;C'_{10}$, 
and observe that $D_p[0,0] = D_p[1,1]  = p$, and $D_p[1,0] = D_p[0,1]  = 1-p$.
Furthermore, $D_p= C'_{01}\;{{}_{1-p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\;C'_{11}$. 
The vulnerability of $D_p$, for uniform $\pi$, is $\mathbb{V}\left[\pi,D_p\right] = 1-\nicefrac{1}{2}p$ for $p\leq\nicefrac{1}{2}$ and $\mathbb{V}\left[\pi,D_p\right] = p$ for $p>\nicefrac{1}{2}$, hence, 
 independently from the choice of the attacker,  the best strategy for the defender is to choose $p=\nicefrac{1}{2}$. 
 Every other value for $p$ gives a strictly higher vulnerability.   
Therefore, the best mixed strategy for the defender is $\sigma^*_{\sf d}$ defined as $\sigma^*_{\sf d}(\lambda_a.0) = \sigma^*_{\sf d}(\lambda_a.1)= \nicefrac{1}{2}$. 
Similarly, the best behavioral strategy for the defender is  $\phi^*_{\sf d}$ defined as $\phi^*_{\sf d}(0) = \phi^*_{\sf d}(1)= \lambda_d. \nicefrac{1}{2}$.
head: environment

label: eg:differ:mixed:behavioral
title: Example
body_md:
\label{eg:differ:mixed:behavioral}
Consider again the example of Section~\ref{sec:running-example}, this time in the setting of Game VI, and still with uniform prior $\pi$.
Let us analyze first the case in which the defender uses behavioral strategies. 
\begin{description}
\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item[Behavioral strategies -- type $\mathcal{A}\rightarrow \mathbb{D}(\mathcal{D})$.] 
If the attacker chooses $0$, which corresponds to committing to the system $C_{00}\;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{10}$, 
then the defender will choose $p=\nicefrac{1}{4}$, which minimizes its vulnerability. 
If he chooses $1$, which corresponds to committing to the system $C_{01}\;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{11}$, then
the defender will choose $p=1$, which minimizes the vulnerability. 
In both cases, the leakage is $p=\nicefrac{1}{2}$, hence both these strategies are solutions to the minimax. 
Note that in the first case the strategy of the defender is probabilistic, while that of the attacker is  pure in both cases. 
\\[-1ex]
\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item[Mixed strategies -- type $\mathbb{D}(\mathcal{A}\,{\rightarrow}\,\mathcal{D})$.] 
Observe that there are only four possible pure strategies  for the defender, 
corresponding to the four functions $f_{ij}:\mathcal{A}\,{\rightarrow}\,\mathcal{D}$ for $i,j\in\{0,1\}$ defined as $f_{ij}(a)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}} i$ if $i=j$ and $f_{ij}(a)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}} a\oplus i$ if $i\neq j$. 
Consider a distribution ${\sigma_{\sf d}}\in \mathbb{D}(\mathcal{A}\,{\rightarrow}\,\mathcal{D})$ and let $p_{ij}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}}  {\sigma_{\sf d}}(f_{ij})$. Then we have $p_{ij} \geq 0$ and $\sum_{i,j} p_{ij} = 1$. 
Observe that the  attacker's  choice $a=0$ determines the matrix $C_{00}\;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\;C_{10}$, with $p= p_{00} + p_{10}$, whose vulnerability is 
 $\mathbb{V}\left[\pi,C_{00}\;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\;C_{10}\right]= 1-\nicefrac{1}{2}p$. 
 On the other hand, the attacker's choice $a=1$ determines the matrix $C_{01}\;{{}_{p'}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\;C_{11}$, with $p'= p_{00} + p_{01}$,  whose vulnerability is 
 $\mathbb{V}\left[\pi,C_{01}\;{{}_{p'}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\;C_{11}\right]= \nicefrac{2}{3}-\nicefrac{2}{3}p$ for $p'\leq \nicefrac{1}{4}$, and $\mathbb{V}\left[\pi,C_{01}\;{{}_{p'}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\;C_{11}\right]= \nicefrac{1}{3}+\nicefrac{2}{3}p$ for $p'> \nicefrac{1}{4}$. 
 By geometrical considerations (cf. the red dashed line in Figure~\ref{fig:graphs}) we can see that the optimal solutions for the defender are all those strategies which 
 give $p=\nicefrac{6}{7}$ and $p'= \nicefrac{1}{7}$,  which yield payoff $\nicefrac{4}{7}$.
 
\end{description}

title: Proposition

$

body_md:
\label{prop:mixed-behavioral}
 For any $\alpha\in \mathbb{D}\mathcal{A}$ and any ${\sigma_{\sf d}} \in\mathbb{D}(\mathcal{A}\,{\rightarrow}\,\mathcal{D})$ there exists ${\phi_{\sf d}} :\mathcal{A}\rightarrow \mathbb{D}(\mathcal{D})$ such that:
\[
\mathbb{V}\left[\pi, {\bigsqcupdot_{a \leftarrow \alpha}}\;{\osum_{d \leftarrow {\phi_{\sf d}}(a)}}  C_{d a} \right] 
\,=\,
\mathbb{V}\left[\pi, {\bigsqcupdot_{a \leftarrow \alpha}}\;{\osum_{\textit{s}_{\sf d} \leftarrow {\sigma_{\sf d}}}}  C_{\textit{s}_{\sf d}(a) a} \right] 
\]

label: prop:uniform-prior-delta
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{prop:uniform-prior-delta}
	Consider the password checker program of
	Algorithm~\ref{alg:pwd-checker} for $n$-bit passwords, where the attacker controls
	the low input to the checker, and the defender controls the
	order in which the bits are checked.
	If the
	prior $\pi$ on possible passwords is uniform, and the payoff is given
	by the posterior Bayes-vulnerability
	$
	\textit{U}(\delta,\alpha) \allowbreak = \allowbreak 
	\operatornamewithlimits{\displaystyle\mathbb{E}}_{\substack{a\leftarrow\alpha\\ }}\hspace{-1ex} \; \mathbb{V}\left[\pi,{{\osum_{d \leftarrow \delta}}} {C_{d a}}\right]
	$,
	then the strategy $(\delta^*,\alpha)$ where $\delta^*$ is \emph{uniform}
	and $\alpha$ is \emph{arbitrary} is
	an equilibrium strategy.
head: environment

label: lemma:equivalent-channels-conditions
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:equivalent-channels-conditions}
Two channels $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ are equivalent iff
every column of $C_{1}$ is a convex combination of 
columns of $C_{2}^{0}$, and every column of $C_{2}$ is a 
convex combination of columns of $C_{1}^{0}$.
head: environment
name: Characterization of channel equivalence~

label: prop:properties-binary-hidden-choice
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:properties-binary-hidden-choice}
For any channels $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ of the same type, 
and any values $0 \leq p,q \leq 1$, 
the binary hidden choice operator satisfies the following 
properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\renewcommand{\alph{enumi})}{\alph{enumi})}

\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item \emph{Idempotency}:
$C_{1} \;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{1} = C_{1}$
\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item \emph{Commutativity}: 
$C_{1} \;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{2} = C_{2} \;{{}_{\overline{p}}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{1}$
\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item \emph{Associativity}: 
$$C_{1} \;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; (C_{2} \;{{}_{q}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{3}) = ( \nicefrac{1}{q} \cdot C_{1} \;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{2}) \;{{}_{q}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; \overline{p} \cdot C_{3}$$ 
if $q \neq 0$.
\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item \emph{Absorption}: 
$$(C_{1} \;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{2}) \;{{}_{q}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; (C_{1} \;{{}_{r}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{2})
= C_{1} \;{{}_{(pq + \overline{q}r)}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\oplus}}}}\; C_{2}.$$
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Properties of the binary hidden choice

label: prop:properties-binary-visible-choice
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:properties-binary-visible-choice}
For any compatible channels $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$, 
and any values $0 \leq p,q \leq 1$, 
the visible choice operator satisfies the following 
properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\renewcommand{\alph{enumi})}{\alph{enumi})}

\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item \emph{Idempotency}: 
$C_{1} \;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\sqcupdot}}}}\; C_{1} \approx C_{1}$
\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item \emph{Commutativity}: 
$C_{1} \;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\sqcupdot}}}}\; C_{2} \approx C_{2} \;{{}_{\overline{p}}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\sqcupdot}}}}\; C_{1}$
\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\setlength{\itemsep}{\wideitemsep}\item \emph{Associativity}: 
$C_{1} \;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\sqcupdot}}}}\; (C_{2} \;{{}_{q}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\sqcupdot}}}}\; C_{3}) \approx ( \nicefrac{1}{q} \cdot C_{1} \;{{}_{p}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\sqcupdot}}}}\; C_{2}) 
\;{{}_{q}{\mathlarger{\mathlarger{\sqcupdot}}}}\; \overline{p} \cdot C_{3}$
if $q \neq 0$.
\end{enumerate}
